The everyday papyri make the flavor vivid — one letter says "have no more anxiety about your household than you would if you were present," showing it was common, practical language for putting someone's mind at ease.

prose.def: Describing something that cannot be changed or altered—fixed, permanent, and settled for good.
prose.article: This adjective means "unchangeable" or "fixed," and as a neuter noun (τὸ ἀμετάθετον) it means "unchangeability" itself. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews 6:17–18, where it describes the permanence of God's purpose and promise; the Septuagint uses it only twice as well, in 3 Maccabees. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions: an inscription of King Attalus II orders his decree placed in temples so it would remain "unmoved and unchangeable for all time," showing the word was everyday language for official, legally binding permanence.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament uses, both folded into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word.

prose.def: Not subject to regret or a change of mind; something that will not be taken back.

prose.def: Refusing to change one's mind or turn from sin; unrepentant and stubbornly set in one's ways.

prose.def: Without measure or limit; describing something not confined to set boundaries.
prose.article: ἄμετρος literally means "without measure," built from the negative prefix and the word for "measure" (μέτρον). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 10 (verses 13 and 15), where Paul uses the phrase "beyond measure" in talking about the proper limits of his sphere of work; the Majority Standard Bible renders both with "influence." prose.def: A Hebrew word of affirmation meaning "truly" or "so be it," used to begin solemn statements or to confirm prayers and praise.
prose.article: Borrowed straight from Hebrew אָמֵן, this indeclinable word carries the sense of something firm and trustworthy. It works two main ways: introducing Jesus' weighty sayings (rendered "truly," about 33% of its 152 occurrences) and closing prayers or doxologies ("amen," about 27%), with many cases blending into the phrase "truly I tell you." A striking detail from the papyri: early Christian scribes wrote it as the numeral 99, the sum of the Greek letters' values, so a prayer could simply end "γένοιτο, 99"—"so be it, Amen."
prose.caution: The boundaries between its "truly," "amen," and "truly I tell you" senses overlap heavily, so the counts reflect translation choices more than sharp distinctions in meaning.

prose.def: Describing someone whose mother is unknown or whose maternal descent is not on record.

prose.def: Free from fault or defect—either a sacrificial animal without physical blemish or a person who is morally blameless.
prose.article: ἄμωμος literally means "without blemish," built from a negative prefix plus μῶμος ("blemish, fault"). It moves between two closely linked uses: the technical sacrificial sense of an animal without physical defect (as of Christ in Hebrews 9:14 and 1 Peter 1:19) and the ethical sense of a person who is morally blameless (Ephesians 1:4, Revelation 14:5). The Septuagint uses it heavily—79 times in 8 books—mostly to render Hebrew תָּמִים ("complete, sound"), 58 of those times, which is why the sacrificial overtone carries into the New Testament; the word also turns up as a personal name and in everyday Koine inscriptions and epitaphs.
